claim: Pigmented immunocytes are specified in vegetal epithelium of sea urchin embryos.
source: In sea urchin embryos, pigmented immunocytes are specified in vegetal epithelium, transition to mesenchyme, migrate, and re-enter ectoderm, distributing in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band, but not ventral ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work (Gibson and Burke, 1985; Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996) in the introduction.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes transition to mesenchyme in sea urchin embryos.
source: In sea urchin embryos, pigmented immunocytes are specified in vegetal epithelium, transition to mesenchyme, migrate, and re-enter ectoderm, distributing in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band, but not ventral ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature (Gibson and Burke, 1985, 1987; Takata and Kominami, 2004).

claim: Pigmented immunocytes migrate in sea urchin embryos.
source: In sea urchin embryos, pigmented immunocytes are specified in vegetal epithelium, transition to mesenchyme, migrate, and re-enter ectoderm, distributing in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band, but not ventral ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature and live imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes re-enter ectoderm in sea urchin embryos.
source: In sea urchin embryos, pigmented immunocytes are specified in vegetal epithelium, transition to mesenchyme, migrate, and re-enter ectoderm, distributing in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band, but not ventral ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by imaging data showing immunocytes inserting into ectoderm.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes distribute in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band but not ventral ectoderm.
source: In sea urchin embryos, pigmented immunocytes are specified in vegetal epithelium, transition to mesenchyme, migrate, and re-enter ectoderm, distributing in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band, but not ventral ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by immunofluorescence imaging in Figure 1A showing pigmented immunocytes in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band but not ventral ectoderm.

claim: Immunocytes express Sp-Eph in sea urchin embryos.
source: Immunocytes express Sp-Eph and Sp-Efn is expressed throughout dorsal and ciliary band ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by immunofluorescence in Figure 3 showing Sp-Eph expression in immunocytes at multiple developmental stages.

claim: Sp-Efn is expressed throughout dorsal and ciliary band ectoderm.
source: Immunocytes express Sp-Eph and Sp-Efn is expressed throughout dorsal and ciliary band ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by immunofluorescence in Figure 1B-E showing Sp-Efn expression in dorsal ectoderm and ciliary band.

claim: Interfering with expression or function of Sp-Eph results in rounded immunocytes entering ectoderm but not adopting a dendritic form.
source: Interfering with expression or function of Sp-Eph results in rounded immunocytes entering ectoderm but not adopting a dendritic form.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by morpholino knockdown and kinase inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 4A,F.

claim: Expressing Sp-Efn throughout embryos permits immunocyte insertion in ventral ectoderm.
source: Expressing Sp-Efn throughout embryos permits immunocyte insertion in ventral ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA injection experiments shown in Figure 4I-M.

claim: In mosaic embryos, immunocytes insert preferentially in ectoderm expressing Sp-Efn.
source: In mosaic embryos, immunocytes insert preferentially in ectoderm expressing Sp-Efn.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by single blastomere injection experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sp-Eph signaling is necessary for epithelial insertion of immunocytes.
source: We conclude that Sp-Eph signaling is necessary and sufficient for epithelial insertion.
evidence: This conclusion is based on loss-of-function experiments showing impaired insertion when Sp-Eph is suppressed (Figure 4).

claim: Sp-Eph signaling is sufficient for epithelial insertion of immunocytes.
source: We conclude that Sp-Eph signaling is necessary and sufficient for epithelial insertion.
evidence: This conclusion is based on gain-of-function experiments showing ectopic insertion when Sp-Efn is expressed in ventral ectoderm (Figure 4I-M).

claim: Immunocytes disperse when Sp-Eph enhances adhesion, causing haptotactic movement to regions of higher ligand abundance.
source: As well, we propose that immunocytes disperse when Sp-Eph enhances adhesion, causing haptotactic movement to regions of higher ligand abundance.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the correlation between Sp-Efn abundance and immunocyte distribution, and the known role of Eph in regulating adhesion.

claim: Eph/Ephrin signaling acts positively to pattern migrating cells in sea urchin embryos.
source: This is a distinctive example of Eph/Ephrin signaling acting positively to pattern migrating cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the experimental data showing attraction rather than repulsion.

claim: Eph receptors usually guide migrations of cells by exclusion from regions expressing Ephrin.
source: Eph receptors usually guide migrations of cells by exclusion from regions expressing Ephrin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior literature (Klein, 2012; Cayuso et al., 2015; Bashaw and Klein, 2010; Bush and Soriano, 2012).

claim: Eph receptors are a family of receptor tyrosine kinases.
source: Eph receptors are a family of receptor tyrosine kinases that are activated by cell surface ligands, Ephrins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Eph receptors are activated by cell surface ligands, Ephrins.
source: Eph receptors are a family of receptor tyrosine kinases that are activated by cell surface ligands, Ephrins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Ephrins are bound to membranes through a glycosylphosphatidylinositol linkage (Ephrin A) or a transmembrane domain (Ephrin B).
source: Ephrins are bound to membranes through a glycosylphosphatidylinositol linkage (Ephrin A) or a transmembrane domain (Ephrin B).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Eph receptors and ligands are found throughout metazoans.
source: The receptors and ligands are found throughout metazoans and they are thought to accompany the evolution of multicellularity (Srivastava et al., 2010; Tischer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Eph receptors and ligands are thought to accompany the evolution of multicellularity.
source: The receptors and ligands are found throughout metazoans and they are thought to accompany the evolution of multicellularity (Srivastava et al., 2010; Tischer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vertebrates have as many as 16 Eph receptors and 8 Ephrins.
source: Vertebrate receptors and ligands are diverse with as many as 16 Eph receptors and 8 Ephrins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: The principal developmental functions of Eph/Ephrin signaling include defining tissue domains and guiding migrating cells or growth cones.
source: The principal developmental functions of Eph/Ephrin signaling include defining tissue domains and guiding migrating cells or growth cones (Klein, 2012; Cayuso et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the best-understood models, Eph receptors repulse cells from regions expressing Ephrin.
source: In the best-understood models, Eph receptors repulse cells from regions expressing Ephrin, or with reverse signaling, where ligand bearing cells respond to receptor binding, Ephrin-expressing cells are repulsed from cells expressing Eph receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge from prior literature.

claim: With reverse signaling, Ephrin-expressing cells are repulsed from cells expressing Eph receptors.
source: In the best-understood models, Eph receptors repulse cells from regions expressing Ephrin, or with reverse signaling, where ligand bearing cells respond to receptor binding, Ephrin-expressing cells are repulsed from cells expressing Eph receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge from prior literature.

claim: Eph and Ephrins regulate cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: Eph and Ephrins regulate cytoskeletal dynamics and often integrate activity of other receptor ligand systems to coordinate adhesive and migratory responses to the environment of the cell (Bashaw and Klein, 2010; Bush and Soriano, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Eph and Ephrins often integrate activity of other receptor ligand systems to coordinate adhesive and migratory responses.
source: Eph and Ephrins regulate cytoskeletal dynamics and often integrate activity of other receptor ligand systems to coordinate adhesive and migratory responses to the environment of the cell (Bashaw and Klein, 2010; Bush and Soriano, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sea urchins have a single Eph receptor (Sp-Eph) and a single Ephrin ligand (Sp-Efn).
source: Genomic studies of sea urchins reveal that there is a single Eph receptor (Sp-Eph) and a single Ephrin ligand (Sp-Efn), making them an attractive model for studies of function (Whittaker et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to genomic studies.

claim: Sea urchins are basal deuterostomes.
source: In addition, urchins are basal deuterostomes, so they provide an opportunity to study the range of morphogenetic mechanisms employed by embryos that share a common ancestor with vertebrates (Drescher, 2002; Mellott and Burke, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: In S. purpuratus, embryos express Sp-Eph and Sp-Efn in two overlapping domains of ectoderm.
source: In S. purpuratus, embryos express Sp-Eph and Sp-Efn in two overlapping domains of ectoderm and Eph/Ephrin signaling appears to have a role in morphogenesis of the ciliary band (Krupke and Burke, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Eph/Ephrin signaling appears to have a role in morphogenesis of the ciliary band in S. purpuratus.
source: In S. purpuratus, embryos express Sp-Eph and Sp-Efn in two overlapping domains of ectoderm and Eph/Ephrin signaling appears to have a role in morphogenesis of the ciliary band (Krupke and Burke, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes have distinctive reddish granules.
source: Pigmented immunocytes are a well-studied cell lineage in urchin embryos because of their distinctive reddish granules and their early specification within the nested rings of endomesodermal cells in the vegetal plate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is a well-known characteristic of these cells.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes are specified early within the nested rings of endomesodermal cells in the vegetal plate.
source: Pigmented immunocytes are a well-studied cell lineage in urchin embryos because of their distinctive reddish granules and their early specification within the nested rings of endomesodermal cells in the vegetal plate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by prior literature.

claim: Specification of pigmented immunocyte precursors begins in cleavage stages when micromeres express Delta.
source: Specification of pigmented immunocyte precursors begins in cleavage stages when micromeres express Delta, which initiates Notch-mediated specification of a non-skeletogenic mesoderm domain in an adjacent ring of veg2-derived blastomeres (Sherwood and McClay, 1999; Sweet et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Delta initiates Notch-mediated specification of a non-skeletogenic mesoderm domain in an adjacent ring of veg2-derived blastomeres.
source: Specification of pigmented immunocyte precursors begins in cleavage stages when micromeres express Delta, which initiates Notch-mediated specification of a non-skeletogenic mesoderm domain in an adjacent ring of veg2-derived blastomeres (Sherwood and McClay, 1999; Sweet et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The non-skeletogenic mesoderm domain is first demarcated by expression of the transcription factor glial cells missing (GCM).
source: This domain is first demarcated by expression of the transcription factor glial cells missing (GCM), which is critical to the specification of pigmented immunocytes in the dorsal half of the domain (Ransick and Davidson, 2006, 2012; Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GCM is critical to the specification of pigmented immunocytes in the dorsal half of the non-skeletogenic mesoderm domain.
source: This domain is first demarcated by expression of the transcription factor glial cells missing (GCM), which is critical to the specification of pigmented immunocytes in the dorsal half of the domain (Ransick and Davidson, 2006, 2012; Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During gastrulation, the pigmented immunocytes transition to mesenchyme and migrate to the ectoderm.
source: During gastrulation, the pigmented immunocytes transition to mesenchyme and migrate to the ectoderm (Gibson and Burke, 1985, 1987; Takata and Kominami, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Once in the ectoderm, pigmented immunocytes adopt a distinctive dendritic form.
source: Once in the ectoderm the cells adopt a distinctive dendritic form and mediate innate responses to pathogens (Solek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes mediate innate responses to pathogens.
source: Once in the ectoderm the cells adopt a distinctive dendritic form and mediate innate responses to pathogens (Solek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes begin to transition from epithelium to mesenchyme during the initial phase of archenteron invagination.
source: Pigmented immunocytes of sea urchin embryos arise in the vegetal mesoderm and begin to transition from epithelium to mesenchyme during the initial phase of archenteron invagination (Gibson and Burke, 1985; Ruffins and Ettensohn, 1996) (Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations and Video 1.

claim: Pigmented immunocyte precursors migrate to the ectoderm where they insert between epithelial cells.
source: The precursors migrate to the ectoderm where they insert between epithelial cells (Videos 2, 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live imaging videos.

claim: In their migratory phase, immunocytes are spherical and have numerous short, spike-like projections.
source: In their migratory phase, immunocytes are spherical and have numerous short, spike-like projections.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on live imaging observations.

claim: When immunocytes insert into epithelium, they extend lamellipodia that spread distally and project numerous filopodia.
source: When immunocytes insert into epithelium, they extend lamellipodia that spread distally and project numerous filopodia (Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Video 4.

claim: Live imaging indicates that when pigmented immunocytes insert into epithelium, they become stationary or move only small distances.
source: Live imaging indicates that when pigmented immunocytes insert into epithelium, they become stationary or move only small distances.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on live imaging observations.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes in the ectoderm continue to actively extend and retract filopodia.
source: However, they continue to actively extend and retract filopodia (Videos 2, 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Videos 2 and 5.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes select a site to insert during their migration from the vegetal plate.
source: As pigmented immunocytes in the ectoderm remain relatively stationary, we concluded that they select a site to insert during their migration from the vegetal plate and that insertion includes a change in immunocyte morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on live imaging observations.

claim: Insertion of pigmented immunocytes includes a change in immunocyte morphology.
source: As pigmented immunocytes in the ectoderm remain relatively stationary, we concluded that they select a site to insert during their migration from the vegetal plate and that insertion includes a change in immunocyte morphology.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on live imaging observations.

claim: The distribution of pigmented immunocytes is stereotypic in that they do not enter ventral ectoderm.
source: The distribution of the pigmented immunocytes is stereotypic in that they do not enter ventral ectoderm and the cells are most dense at the tips of larval arms (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes are most dense at the tips of larval arms.
source: The distribution of the pigmented immunocytes is stereotypic in that they do not enter ventral ectoderm and the cells are most dense at the tips of larval arms (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The density of immunocytes is graded in the dorsal ectoderm.
source: As well, the density of immunocytes is graded in the dorsal ectoderm (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1F.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes are most dense at the tip of larval body and along the edge of the ciliary band.
source: Pigmented immunocytes are most dense at the tip of larval body and along the edge of the ciliary band.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from Figure 1.

claim: Counts of pigmented immunocytes in a series of 5 midline quadrants arrayed along the axis from the animal pole to the vertex indicate a parabolic distribution.
source: Counts of pigmented immunocytes in a series of 5 midline quadrants arrayed along the axis from the animal pole to the vertex indicate a parabolic distribution (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1G.

claim: Sp-Efn is not expressed in the ventral ectoderm.
source: Sp-Efn is not expressed in ventral ectoderm, but is expressed in the ciliary band and dorsal ectoderm and it appears to be most abundant at the tips of the larval arms (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Sp-Efn is expressed in the ciliary band and dorsal ectoderm.
source: Sp-Efn is not expressed in ventral ectoderm, but is expressed in the ciliary band and dorsal ectoderm and it appears to be most abundant at the tips of the larval arms (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Sp-Efn appears to be most abundant at the tips of the larval arms.
source: Sp-Efn is not expressed in ventral ectoderm, but is expressed in the ciliary band and dorsal ectoderm and it appears to be most abundant at the tips of the larval arms (Figure 1B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Measurements of fluorescence intensity per pixel in 5 evenly spaced quadrants along the axis from the animal pole domain to the vertex indicate that there is a gradient of Sp-Efn abundance in the dorsal ectoderm.
source: Measurements of fluorescence intensity per pixel in 5 evenly spaced quadrants along the axis from the animal pole domain to the vertex indicate that there is a gradient of Sp-Efn abundance in the dorsal ectoderm (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 1H.

claim: There is a correlation in the distribution of pigmented immunocytes and the abundance of Sp-Efn.
source: These observations show a correlation in the distribution of pigmented immunocytes and the abundance of Sp-Efn, suggesting a role for Sp-Efn in localization of these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the data in Figure 1.

claim: The correlation between pigmented immunocyte distribution and Sp-Efn abundance suggests a role for Sp-Efn in localization of these cells.
source: These observations show a correlation in the distribution of pigmented immunocytes and the abundance of Sp-Efn, suggesting a role for Sp-Efn in localization of these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the correlation observed.

claim: Fixation with PEM results in immunolocalization of Sp-Efn on the basal surface of ectodermal cells.
source: Fixation with PEM, a buffer designed to stabilize cytoskeletal structure (Vielkind and Swierenga, 1989) results in immunolocalization of Sp-Efn on the basal surface of ectodermal cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Sp-Efn is abundant on long, thin projections that radiate into the blastocoel.
source: In addition to small cytoplasmic granules, Sp-Efn is abundant on long, thin projections that radiate into the blastocoel (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The processes expressing Sp-Efn are unbranched, up to 15 µm in length and 0.1–0.2 µm in diameter.
source: The processes are unbranched, up to 15 µm in length and 0.1–0.2 µm in diameter (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Fixation with ice-cold methanol, or buffered formaldehyde solutions, localizes Sp-Efn to dorsal ectodermal cells, but does not preserve the basal processes.
source: Notably, fixation with ice-cold methanol, or buffered formaldehyde solutions, localizes Sp-Efn to dorsal ectodermal cells, but does not preserve the basal processes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on experimental observations.

claim: Localization with apical markers, spectrin or actin, and DIC imaging confirms that Sp-Efn is abundant on processes radiating into the blastocoel.
source: Localization with apical markers, spectrin or actin, and DIC imaging to establish the position of the basal surface, confirms that Sp-Efn is abundant on processes radiating into the blastocoel (Figure 2D–J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2D-J.

claim: Co-localization of Sp-Efn with filamentous actin indicates that the processes contain actin.
source: Co-localization of Sp-Efn with filamentous actin indicates that the processes contain actin (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2H-J.

claim: In sequential images captured at a rate of 4 frames per minute, fluorescent processes emanating from the basal surfaces of ectodermal cells are apparent in embryos expressing membrane GFP.
source: In sequential images captured at a rate of 4 frames per minute, fluorescent processes emanating from the basal surfaces of ectodermal cells are apparent (Figure 2K,L, Video 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 2K,L and Video 6.

claim: When embryos express the actin-binding Lifeact-GFP, thin fluorescent projections emanate from the bases of ectodermal cells.

claim: The projections are common on the basal surfaces of dorsal and ventral ectoderm, but not associated with endodermal epithelia.
source: The projections are common on the basal surfaces of dorsal and ventral ectoderm, but not associated with endodermal epithelia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from live imaging.

claim: Sp-Efn protein is presented on membrane-delimited, actin-containing, cytonemal processes on the basal surfaces of ectodermal cells.
source: We concluded from these studies that Sp-Efn protein is presented on membrane-delimited, actin-containing, cytonemal processes on the basal surfaces of ectodermal cells.

claim: In hatched blastulae, cells in the vegetal plate that are immunoreactive with the immunocyte-specific antibody Sp1 are also immunoreactive with anti-Sp-Eph.
source: In hatched blastulae, cells in the vegetal plate that are immunoreactive with the immunocyte-specific antibody Sp1 (Gibson and Burke, 1985), are also immunoreactive with anti-Sp-Eph (Krupke and Burke, 2014) (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Sp-Efn is present on the basal surfaces of ectodermal cells at the hatched blastula stage.
source: Sp-Efn is present at the same time on the basal surfaces of ectodermal cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 3D.

claim: By 36 hr, presumptive pigmented immunocytes are mesenchyme within the blastocoel and continue to express Sp-Eph.
source: By 36 hr, presumptive pigmented immunocytes are mesenchyme within the blastocoel and continue to express Sp-Eph (Figure 3E–G).

claim: In gastrulae (42 hr), pigmented immunocytes have migrated to the basal surface of dorsal and ciliary band ectoderm.
source: In gastrulae (42 hr), pigmented immunocytes have migrated to the basal surface of dorsal and ciliary band ectoderm (Figure 3H–J) and they extend projections into the ectoderm.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes extend projections into the ectoderm in gastrulae.
source: In gastrulae (42 hr), pigmented immunocytes have migrated to the basal surface of dorsal and ciliary band ectoderm (Figure 3H–J) and they extend projections into the ectoderm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 3H-J.

claim: The projections of pigmented immunocytes can extend beyond the apical ectodermal surface.
source: The projections can extend beyond the apical ectodermal surface (insets Figure 3H–J, Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 3H-J insets and Video 5.

claim: In early plutei (72 hr), pigmented immunocytes have a typical dendritic morphology in which cells have multiple lamellipodia-like projections between ectodermal cells immediately beneath apical junctions.
source: In early plutei (72 hr), pigmented immunocytes have a typical dendritic morphology in which cells have multiple lamellipodia-like projections between ectodermal cells immediately beneath apical junctions (Figure 3K–M).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Figure 3K-M.

claim: Pigmented immunocytes continue to express Sp-Eph in early pluteus stages.
source: The pigmented immunocytes continue to express Sp-Eph in early pluteus stages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations from Figure 3.

claim: Sp-Eph is expressed by pigmented immunocyte from the time of their release from the vegetal plate throughout early larval development.
source: These findings indicate Sp-Eph is expressed by pigmented immunocyte from the time of their release from the vegetal plate throughout early larval development.

claim: Suppressing expression of Sp-Eph produces embryos that gastrulate and have defects in the ciliary band.
source: Suppressing expression of Sp-Eph produces embryos that gastrulate and have defects in the ciliary band (Krupke and Burke, 2014) (Figure 4A).

claim: At 40 hr there is no difference in the number of Sp1 immunoreactive cells between control and experimental treatments (NVP or Sp-Eph MO1).
source: Immunocyte precursors migrate to the ectoderm and at 40 hr there is no difference in the number of Sp1 immunoreactive cells between control and experimental treatments (Figure 4A,E).

claim: At 72 hr pigmented immunocyte abundance is significantly reduced in NVP treated (p<0.0001) or Sp-Eph MO1 injected (p = 0.009) embryos.
source: However at 72 hr pigmented immunocyte abundance is significantly reduced in NVP treated (p<0.0001) or Sp-Eph MO1 injected (p = 0.009) embryos (Figure 4E).

claim: In 72 hr embryos injected with Sp-EphMO1, the immunocytes are larger in diameter, with fewer lamellipodia and shorter filopodia than embryos injected with a control morpholino.

claim: In embryos treated with NVP or derived from eggs injected with Sp-Eph MO1, a significantly larger proportion of immunocytes are within the blastocoel.
source: As well, in embryos treated with NVP or derived from eggs injected with Sp-Eph MO1, a significantly larger proportion of immunocytes are within the blastocoel (Figure 4G).

claim: Interfering with Eph signaling results in immunocytes that are impaired in their ability to insert into the ectoderm and do not transition to the characteristic dendritic morphology.
source: Thus, interfering with Eph signaling results in immunocytes that are impaired in their ability to insert into the ectoderm and do not transition to the characteristic dendritic morphology.

claim: Immunocytes that remain in the blastocoel of Sp-Eph MO injected embryos commonly have fragmented nuclei and reduced Sp1 intensity.
source: In addition, immunocytes that remain in the blastocoel of Sp-Eph MO injected embryos commonly have fragmented nuclei and reduced Sp1 intensity.

source: When half of the embryo expresses Sp-Efn ectopically there are more immunocytes inserted in ectoderm on the injected half of the embryo than on the uninjected half or the GFP injected controls (Figure 5A–C,M, Video 8).
